newsitem.title: USA: Airline stocks tumble amid Q2 concerns, downgrades. [CORRECTED 22:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Airline stocks tumble amid Q2 concerns, downgrades. [CORRECTED 22:50 GMT]

text.p: U.S. airline stocks tumbled Tuesday after several brokerage firms trimmed earnings estimates, citing pressure from fare sales and the return of a federal ticket tax.

The American Stock Exchange airline index lost nearly 16 points or 3.3 percent to 460. The Dow Jones transportation average slipped 1.33 percent to 2663 points, compared with a 0.61 percent gain in the Dow industrials.
Hardest hit were AMR Corp, the parent of American Airlines, which fell 5.4 percent or 5-3/8 points to 94-1/8, and Continental Airlines Inc, off 1-7/8 points to 34-1/2.

"All the companies are talking estimates down," said Helane Becker, an airline analyst with Smith Barney. Becker said her earnings forecasts have been lower than the Wall Street consensus because of concerns about the federal passenger excise tax, which returned in March.
"I'm surprised the companies weren't more cautious in their conference calls," when they released their first quarter results and made projections about the second quarter, Becker said.

The 10 percent excise tax was absent throughout the second quarter last year, allowing airlines to cull funds that normally go to the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration. Without those extra funds this year, comparisons with last year's second quarter will be more difficult, analysts said.
The impact of the excise tax is not a surprise. But the combination of the tax and recent fare sales have made the calendar second quarter outlook less rosy, analysts said.

Lehman Brothers trimmed earnings estimates for several airlines on Tuesday, saying revenue weakness will sharply cut into profits at Delta Air Lines Inc, Northwest Airlines Corp and Trans World Airlines Inc.
(Corrects from "downgraded several airline stocks" to "trimmed earnings estimates for several airlines".)
First Boston analyst Tom Schreier said recent fare sales also ate away at second quarter revenues. The industry sales generated air traffic at the expense of revenue yield, he said.
A fare sale by Delta "put too much inventory on sale at too low a price," Schreier said.
The growth in the lower-yielding leisure sector has hit all airlines. Although high-yield business travel remains steady, the growth has been in low-fare leisure travel, analysts said.

On Monday, Delta said unit revenues for the fourth fiscal quarter ending in June would be only slightly ahead of levels recorded a year ago. A Delta spokesman cited the return of the excise tax and said growth in leisure travel had hurt yields.
Delta lost 3-3/4 to 88 in afternoon trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Continental said it agreed to buy 35 widebody aircraft from Boeing Co through the year 2004 and buy additional Boeing aircraft over the next 20 years.

Separately, British Airways Plc Chairman Sir Colin Marshall said he had no timetable on when BA's proposed alliance with American Airlines may be approved. British Air also retiterated its stance that it could forego the alliance if regulators required the airlines to pay a burdensome price.
Although British Air's comments were not new, the statements added to a string of less-than-positive sentiment on American and the rest of the airline industry, analysts said.
"There's a convergence of negative news and just no positive news. It all came together today ... I'd say the whole reaction is an overreaction," Schreier said.
Separately, on Monday the U.S. House Ways and Means Committee proposed restructuring domestic air travel taxes and boosting fees on international travel.
